blogs.title: The Dosing Gap: Why Your Adult Anaphylaxis Auto-Injectors Might Be Underdosing Your Patients
blogs.description: This post dissects the critical discrepancy between guideline-recommended epinephrine dosing (0.5 mg for adults >50 kg) and the ubiquitous 0.3 mg auto-injectors found in many hospitals and homes. Using the case of a 104 kg patient who required escalating doses to control multiphasic shocks, we analyze recent data suggesting that initial underdosing correlates with higher rates of treatment failure and ICU admission. We will discuss practical strategies for bridging this gap in the ED, including when to bypass auto-injectors for manual IM dosing and how to educate patients on discharge prescriptions.

blogs.title: Beyond the 4-Hour Rule: Risk-Stratifying Observation Periods for Biphasic and Multiphasic Anaphylaxis
blogs.description: Traditional teaching often suggests a 4-to-6-hour observation window for anaphylaxis, but this case of four distinct relapse episodes over 12 hours challenges that dogma. This article reviews the conflicting literature on biphasic reaction incidence (ranging from 0.4% to 23%) and evaluates proposed risk factors such as severity of initial presentation, hypotension, and requirement for multiple epinephrine doses. We will propose a pragmatic, tiered monitoring framework inspired by the UK Resuscitation Council guidelines to help clinicians decide who needs short-stay observation versus ICU-level surveillance without overwhelming emergency resources.

blogs.title: The Steroid Myth Persists: Re-evaluating Adjunctive Therapies in Complex Anaphylactic Courses
blogs.description: Despite mounting evidence that corticosteroids do not prevent biphasic reactions and may increase adverse events, they remain a staple in many anaphylaxis protocols—as seen in this case where both prednisone and dexamethasone were administered after relapse began. This post dives into the 2017 systematic review and subsequent studies debunking the prophylactic utility of steroids in anaphylaxis. We will explore why the 'just in case' mentality persists among clinicians and offer script alternatives for managing patient expectations while adhering to evidence-based medicine that prioritizes epinephrine and fluids alone.

blogs.title: When Anaphylaxis Won't Quit: Managing Refractory and Multiphasic Episodes Without a Playbook
blogs.description: While refractory anaphylaxis (lack of response to epi) has defined algorithms, multiphasic anaphylaxis (recurrence after resolution) lacks clear management guidelines. This post analyzes the therapeutic tension faced in this case: initiating a preemptive IV epinephrine infusion versus an expectant approach with repeated IM dosing. We will discuss the physiological rationale for each strategy, the risks of overtreatment vs. undertreatment, and how to navigate decision-making in the absence of Level 1 evidence when a patient experiences multiple waves of shock within a single admission.

blogs.title: The Hidden Culprit: Screening for Systemic Mastocytosis in Severe or Atypical Anaphylaxis
blogs.description: This case highlights a crucial diagnostic pivot: a patient with multiphasic anaphylaxis triggered by clarithromycin was found to have elevated baseline tryptase and features suggestive of undiagnosed systemic mastocytosis. This article serves as a clinical guide on when to suspect underlying mast cell disorders in patients presenting with severe, idiopathic, or multiphasic anaphylaxis. We will outline the proper timing for acute vs. baseline tryptase sampling (often missed in the chaos of resuscitation), interpret WHO diagnostic criteria limitations, and discuss long-term implications for patients who may require specialized allergology follow-up and different avoidance strategies.
